items.questionAndWhy: Can feedback from a generative AI tool improve novice teachers' instructional-design skill as much as teacher-led feedback? Understanding equivalence and trade-offs is useful for designing practitioner education.
items.whatTheyDid: A Chinese university study randomized 46 pre-service teachers to learning sequences that included human–AI and teacher–student collaboration; 36 completed an eight-week crossover analysis. Expert-rated lesson plans were assessed at baseline, four weeks and eight weeks, using DeepSeek-V2 for AI feedback.
items.whatTheyFound: Both modes coincided with improved design scores over time, but their overall scores did not differ significantly. Specific dimensions and learner experiences varied. Ten withdrawals and an author-developed evaluation scale limit certainty; the setting was a single university and the short follow-up did not test long-term retention.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX training could compare AI and instructor feedback using blinded work-product scoring, later unaided retention and performance transfer. The study supports testing both modes, not claiming that AI replaces teachers or has identical effects in operational training.
items.streamTitle: AI and teacher feedback produced similar overall training gains in a small randomized crossover
items.streamSummary: An eight-week study analyzed 36 pre-service teachers after 46 were recruited: instructional-design skill rose in both human–AI and teacher-guided settings, without a reliable overall difference. Attrition, one institution and short follow-up constrain transfer.
items.attribution: Wang, Zhang, Zheng, Jiang, Gao and Li — Frontiers in Psychology (crossover educational experiment; November 17, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: When does following a majority help, and when should learners discount it because demonstrators have different incentives? Group identity and payoff alignment may alter the informational value of identical social signals.
items.whatTheyDid: An incentivized experimental design separated demonstrators learning from private feedback from social learners who observed only choices. It varied ingroup/outgroup cues and whether demonstrator incentives aligned with the learner's, and ran participant samples in Switzerland and Kenya. Cognitive-load conditions also tested processing limits.
items.whatTheyFound: Performance was strongest when demonstrators' incentives aligned, especially for minimally defined ingroup demonstrators. Cognitive load impaired memory but did not reliably change social-information use. Strategies were heterogeneous in both locations and more dispersed in Kenya. These results concern experimental option choices, not natural political conformity.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX social-influence models should represent source incentive compatibility and perceived group membership separately from raw message popularity. An operational extension would test whether these signals predict observed audience uptake; the experiment does not establish field persuasion.
items.streamTitle: Social learning responded to payoff alignment and group identity, not majority size alone
items.streamSummary: In incentivized Swiss and Kenyan experiments, the same majority cue was interpreted differently depending on demonstrators' payoff alignment and ingroup status. Cognitive load affected memory but not reliably social-information use; human strategies varied by site.
items.attribution: von Flüe, Vogt and Efferson — Journal of Experimental Psychology: General (cross-population incentivized experiments; online August 31, November issue)

items.questionAndWhy: Does sharing a sequential risky task with another person alter choices and processing of gains and losses? Responsibility and audience context may change both risk behavior and feedback evaluation.
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers used EEG event-related potentials during an individual-versus-dyadic, turn-taking Balloon Analogue Risk Task with gain/loss framing. They compared risk behavior, feedback-related negativity and P3b responses under different feedback valences.
items.whatTheyFound: Participants took more risks in the dyadic than individual setting and reduced risk after negative rather than positive feedback. Negative-feedback FRN was enhanced in dyads, whereas P3b was generally larger individually. A proposed framing-by-context P3b pattern was not significant after multiple-comparison correction. The task is controlled, not an actual organizational decision.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX team-decision experiments could measure how shared responsibility changes risk and feedback adaptation instead of assuming that group choices equal aggregated individual preferences. Field generalization to wargames or real operational choices remains untested.
items.streamTitle: Dyadic decision-making increased risk taking and changed neural feedback responses
items.streamSummary: A November 11 EEG study found more risk-taking during dyadic than solo sequential decisions, with differing FRN and P3b feedback responses; one framing interaction did not survive correction. Evidence is from a laboratory risk task.
items.attribution: Li, Gao and Li — Biological Psychology (dyadic behavioral/EEG experiment; November 11, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: How should public institutions maintain accurate information when users receive AI-generated answers rather than clicking official pages? This creates an information-integrity and public-service communication problem.
items.whatTheyDid: UK Government Communications issued and updated guidance organized around PRIME: Plan, Respond, Implement, Monitor and Evaluate. It describes content audits, direct answers to public queries, structured information, monitoring of generated responses and continuous error evaluation. The page was first issued October 20 and updated November 17.
items.whatTheyFound: The source documents a government communication framework and cited trends in AI-mediated search. It does not demonstrate that applying PRIME reduces misinformation, changes public trust or ensures that a particular model returns correct answers. It is prescriptive operational guidance rather than an evaluated field intervention.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX strategic-communication assessments could test answer accuracy, attribution to authoritative sources, omissions and changes after corrections across AI search services. Separate discoverability and source citation from belief or behavior effects; PRIME itself remains unevaluated for these outcomes.
items.streamTitle: UK government updated guidance for communicating accurately through AI-generated search answers
items.streamSummary: Updated November 17, the UK Government Communications PRIME framework recommends auditing public information, structuring answers for AI search and monitoring errors. It specifies a workflow, not proven improvement in trust or audience outcomes.
items.attribution: UK Government Communications — Strengthening public trust in the age of AI-powered search (official guidance; published October 20, updated November 17, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Does adding specialized AI agents and deterministic safety rules improve complex recommendations beyond a single language model? A rigorous comparison must separate apparent performance from leakage and overfitting.
items.whatTheyDid: SMARTriage AI combined specialist language-model agents with rule-based admission/discharge gates. Initial prompts were iterated roughly 30 times on the same retrospective cohort of 469 adult hospital encounters, without a holdout. After peer review, the authors locked a redesigned version and compared it with single-agent baselines on the same cohort.
items.whatTheyFound: The initial version appeared 88.2% accurate with 96.1% admission recall, but evaluation reused development cases and physician notes could leak disposition. Under locked v2 evaluation, AUC was 0.794 versus 0.821–0.823 for single-agent comparators; the multi-agent system did not outperform them. There was no external or prospective validation.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX research agents, increasing agent count or adding rules cannot be assumed to improve decisions. Require untouched evaluation sets, source-information leakage checks and single-agent baselines. These are clinical benchmark lessons, not demonstrated outcomes in behavioral analysis.
items.streamTitle: Redesigned multi-agent decision support failed to outperform a single model after stricter testing
items.streamSummary: A November 18 retrospective SMARTriage study found initial 88.2% apparent accuracy was vulnerable to development reuse and documentation leakage; locked re-evaluation favored simpler single-agent baselines by AUC. No clinical field utility was established.
items.attribution: Tsafrir, Arama, Ben Haim and Saban — Scientific Reports (retrospective AI decision-support evaluation; November 18, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can a live-content moderation pipeline combine visual violence, harmful speech, sound events and related text rather than classify each stream independently? The concrete problem is recognizing potentially harmful material across modalities in real time.
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers integrated DeepLabV3+, Faster R-CNN, Wav2Vec 2.0, CNN sound models and BERT into a priority-scheduled video/audio/text moderation system. A Content Sentinel component supports actions such as skipping flagged segments. The authors report an overall test detection accuracy of 98.33%.
items.whatTheyFound: The paper demonstrates an implemented prototype and its reported benchmark accuracy, not independently established platform-scale effectiveness. The abstract does not establish performance across languages, rare categories, adversarial edits or real moderation workloads. False positives and differential error rates remain important constraints.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX information-environment work could evaluate multimodal threat-detection pipelines on independently labeled, representative content and measure per-category false positives. Detection of unsafe content is not detection of coordinated influence or proof that user harm was reduced.
items.streamTitle: Multimodal moderation prototype combined video, audio and text threat detection
items.streamSummary: A November 18 Scientific Reports prototype combined vision, speech, audio and text models and reported 98.33% overall detection accuracy. Real-platform robustness, category-specific errors and changes in harm were not independently demonstrated.
items.attribution: Manikandan, Swarna and Nivetha — Scientific Reports (multimodal content-moderation prototype; November 18, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can a generative agent-based simulation do more than reproduce a plausible collective pattern by explicitly comparing candidate behavioral rules? The challenge is connecting local decisions to collective outcomes while controlling other simulation conditions.
items.whatTheyDid: RePair calibrates a baseline simulation, encodes a hypothesized local decision mechanism as a natural-language rule, registers an outcome prediction, then compares matched simulations with the same models, profiles, initial states and schedules. It examines configuration variation and behavior traces across four simulation worlds.
items.whatTheyFound: Rule interventions generated measurable changes in simulated collective outcomes, and trace analysis helped examine whether intended intermediate behavior occurred. Equivalent rules and model settings could affect conclusions. These are within-simulator comparisons, not validated identification of mechanisms in human populations.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX causal COA simulation, this suggests a bounded test of alternative agent-level hypotheses using paired initializations, semantic-prompt sensitivity and trace evidence. Prospective comparison with measured intervention outcomes is still needed before forecasting success probabilities.
items.streamTitle: Paired interventions in LLM-agent simulations tested candidate micro-to-macro mechanisms
items.streamSummary: RePair matched interventions on hypothesized behavioral rules across four simulated social worlds, examining aggregate changes and agent traces. It strengthens simulator-internal causal testing but does not establish human causal validity.
items.attribution: Liu, Shang, Bhat and Jin — arXiv preprint, Exploring Causal Mechanisms with Generative Agent-Based Models (simulation methods; September 21, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: How can verifiers tell whether a signed media artifact originated with a recognized publisher when signature technologies use different certificate types? The challenge is reliable publisher identity checking across media workflows.
items.whatTheyDid: IPTC updated its Verified News Publisher technical annex November 16. It describes a primary X.509 end-entity publisher certificate list and a separate list for C2PA Conformance Program claim-signing products. The annex defines when each list may be used for C2PA claims and CAWG identity assertions.
items.whatTheyFound: The policy now specifies a machine-readable certificate-validation route and distinguishes organization identity assertions from product claim signatures. It is technical policy, not an evaluation showing adoption, lower misinformation exposure or that signed content is factually true. Correct cryptographic signature verification establishes provenance under the trust framework, not truth.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX media-integrity assessments can record claimed publisher identity, signature-chain validity, provenance continuity and factual accuracy as separate fields. Testing how users interpret provenance badges is a separate behavioral experiment, not a result of the annex.
items.streamTitle: IPTC clarified which publisher certificates validate signed media provenance
items.streamSummary: An IPTC technical annex updated November 16 defines machine-readable publisher certificate lists for C2PA and CAWG checks. It enables more precise provenance verification but does not certify factual truth or demonstrate audience effects.
items.attribution: International Press Telecommunications Council — Verified News Publisher Policy: Technical Annex (official technical standard; updated November 16, 2026)
